title: Have You Ever? Shall We?
overview: Ask and answer: Have you ever climbed a mountain? Give an idea with Shall we…? and ask about a plan with Will you…? Read rules with must, and say what you could do in the past. Ask What kind of…? How long…? How far…?
learningPath: The lesson: listen, then say each line.
Words: 24 words about nature, trying things and plans.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you first.
Reading: two short texts and a sign at a park.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, then listen back.
Writing: write about you. Made-up answers are fine.
Practice: six exercises. Check each one with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. Then look at My progress.
lectureScript:
Hello! This is Unit 18.
In this unit, you talk about things you have done.
You give ideas, you ask about plans, and you read rules.
Listen to this question.
Have you ever climbed a mountain?
Ever means: at any time, before now.
Yes, I have. Or: No, I haven't.
Haven't is have not, in one word.
I have climbed a mountain.
I have never climbed a mountain.
With he and she, say has: She has climbed a mountain.
After have, the word takes a new form.
Many are like the past: climb, climbed. Try, tried. Taste, tasted.
Some change: see, seen. Eat, eaten. Grow, grown. Win, won. Fly, flown.
For a place, say been: Have you ever been to a desert?
Your answers can be true or made up.
One more thing. A Have you ever question has no time word in it.
With last year or yesterday, use the past: I climbed it last year.
Now ideas and plans.
You and a friend want a day out.
Say: Shall we go to the beach?
Shall we gives an idea for you and the other person.
Answer: Good idea! Or: OK, sure. Or: Maybe later.
To ask about a plan, say Will you.
Will you come on Saturday?
Yes, I will. No, I won't.
Won't is will not.
Now rules.
Must says: you need to do this. It is a rule.
On a bike, you must wear a helmet.
Must not says: do not do this.
At the pool, you must not run.
After must, the word stays the same, like after can.
Not: you must to wear. Say: you must wear.
Now could.
Could is can, in the past.
Now I can swim. When I was six, I couldn't swim.
When I was ten, I could ride a bike.
Listen to could. The l is quiet. Could sounds like good.
Last, three new questions.
What kind of music do you like? I like film music.
Here, kind means a group of the same things.
A forest is one kind of place. A desert is another kind.
How long is the film? Two hours.
How long is the bridge? Three hundred metres.
How long asks how much time, or how many metres from end to end.
How far is the beach? It is five hundred metres from here.
How far asks: is it near or far from here?
Now you. Say one thing you have done.
Say one thing you have never done.
Then give an idea: Shall we go to the lake?
Now go to Words. Goodbye!

outcomes.outcome: Ask and answer Have you ever…? questions, and say what you have done and have never done.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 1 practice self-checked; Speaking 1 and 2 recordings against their checklists; Quiz items 1 and 2.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask Have you ever…? and answer Yes, I have or No, I haven't.

outcomes.outcome: Write about experiences with have or has and the right form of the word: tasted, seen, eaten, been.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 1, seven or more of eight; Writing 1 checklist; Quiz items 3 and 4.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write: I have tasted it. I have never been there.

outcomes.outcome: Give an idea with Shall we…?, ask about a plan with Will you…?, and answer both.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice; Practice 3; Speaking 5 recording, including a new A line of your own; Quiz items 5 and 6.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say Shall we…? and answer Will you…?

outcomes.outcome: Read short texts about places in nature and a sign of rules, and find what you must and must not do.
outcomes.evidence: Reading 1 to 3 questions; Pattern 3 practice; Practice 2 and Practice 4; Quiz items 7, 8 and 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can read a sign and say what I must do.

outcomes.outcome: Say what you could and couldn't do in the past, and say could with a quiet l.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 4 practice; Practice 5; Speaking 4 recording; Writing 2 checklist; Quiz items 9 and 10.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say: When I was six, I couldn't swim.

outcomes.outcome: Understand and answer questions with What kind of…?, How long…? and How far…?, and ask them.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 3 and Speaking 6 recordings; Pattern 5 practice; Practice 6; Quiz item 11.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can answer What kind of…? How long…? How far…?

outcomes.outcome: Write a short message with an idea, a question and a rule, and check it against a list.
outcomes.evidence: Writing 3 and Writing 4 against their checklists; the assignment message.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write a message with Shall we…? and a rule.

words.meaning: Very, very big water with salt in it.
words.example: The sea is blue and very big.
practice: Have you ever seen the sea?
There are many fish in the sea.
The sea is cold in the morning.
The sea has salt in its water.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor two things about the sea: its colour, and hot or cold. Ask it for one more describing word for the sea.

words.meaning: A very tall place in nature, much bigger than a building.
words.example: The mountain has snow at the top.
practice: Have you ever climbed a mountain?
It is cold at the top of the mountain.
We could see the mountain from the window.
How far is the mountain from here?
words.starter: At the top of the mountain, …
words.tutor: Ask the tutor How far is the mountain? and How long is the walk to the top? Then answer both for a made-up mountain.

words.meaning: A long line of water. It goes to the sea or to a lake.
words.example: The river goes to the sea.
practice: How long is the river?
There is a bridge over the river.
We walked next to the river after lunch.
Small fish live in the river.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor: How long is the river? and How far is the river? Ask it to show you the difference with a made-up river.

words.meaning: Big water in one place. It is not the sea, and it is smaller.
words.example: We had lunch next to the lake.
practice: The lake is very cold in the morning.
Shall we walk to the lake together?
How far is the lake from here?
There are small fish in the lake.
words.tutor: Say to the tutor: Shall we go to the lake? Ask it to answer, then ask you one question about the lake.

words.meaning: A big place with a lot of trees.
words.example: Many animals live in the forest.
practice: Have you ever walked in a forest?
The forest is green and quiet.
What kind of trees are in the forest?
You must not cut the trees in the forest.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you can see in a forest. Ask it for one rule for a forest with must not.

words.meaning: A place in the sea or in a lake, with water on every side.
words.example: The island is small and green.
practice: Have you ever been to an island?
You can see the island from the beach.
The island is 800 metres from the beach.
Island: the s is quiet.
words.tutor: Say island to the tutor five times. Ask it if the s was quiet each time, as it should be.

words.meaning: The place next to the sea where you can sit, walk and swim.
words.example: We walked on the beach in the evening.
practice: Shall we go to the beach on Sunday?
How far is the beach from here?
The beach is hot in the afternoon.
You must not ride a bike on the beach.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor two things you can do at the beach. Then say one thing you must not do.

words.meaning: A big place with not much rain and not many plants.
words.example: It does not rain much in the desert.
practice: Have you ever been to a desert?
The desert is hot in the day and cold at night.
Some plants can grow in the desert.
What kind of animals live in the desert?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor: What kind of animals live in the desert? Then tell it one thing about a desert with it is.

words.meaning: A thing that lives and moves, like a fish or a bird.
words.example: Many animals need water every day.
practice: What kind of animal is it? It is a fish.
There are big animals in the sea.
One animal, two animals.
Some animals live in the desert.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor your favourite animal, and one place where it lives. Ask it: What kind of animal is it?

words.meaning: A green thing that grows. It needs water and sun.
words.example: This plant needs water every day.
practice: Have you ever grown a plant?
Some plants can grow in the desert.
You must not walk on the plants.
The plant is next to the window.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor two things a plant needs. Ask it for one more, and say all three in one line with and.

words.meaning: A very big, tall plant. It can live for many years.
words.example: There is a big tree in the park.
practice: Have you ever climbed a tree?
What kind of tree is that? It is an apple tree.
The tree is taller than the building.
Trees grow slowly.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor: What kind of tree is that? Listen to its answer, then describe a tree near you, real or made up.

words.meaning: At any time, before now.
words.example: Have you ever seen a desert?
practice: Have you ever tasted a new fruit?
Has she ever won a game?
No, never. I have never been there.
Ever goes after you, in the question.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor three questions with Have you ever…? Then ask it to ask you three. Your answers can be made up.

words.meaning: Do or eat a thing for the first time.
words.example: Shall we try the new café?
practice: Have you ever tried fish for breakfast?
I tried a new game yesterday.
Try this bread. It is very good.
Try, tried: the y changes to i.
words.tutor: Type tried for the tutor. Ask it to check the y changed to i. Then use tried in a Have you ever question.

words.meaning: Try food or drink in your mouth.
words.example: Taste the rice. Does it need salt?
practice: Have you ever tasted this fruit?
This coffee tastes good.
Taste it first, then add salt.
I tasted a new kind of bread today.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor one food that tastes good to you and one that doesn't. True or made up is fine.

words.meaning: Move up in the sky, like a bird or a plane.
words.example: Birds fly over the lake.
practice: Can this bird fly?
The plane flies over the sea.
A small bird has flown into the tree.
Fly, flown: after have, say flown.
words.starter: A bird can fly over the …
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three things that can fly and one animal that can't fly. Ask it to check your list.

words.meaning: Go up a tree or a mountain with your hands and legs.
words.example: She climbed the mountain in five hours.
practice: Have you ever climbed a tree?
When I was ten, I could climb trees.
Climb: the b is quiet.
You must not climb on the wall.
words.tutor: Say climb and climbed to the tutor. Ask it if the b was quiet both times.

words.meaning: Be number one in a game.
words.example: We won the football game.
practice: Have you ever won a game?
Win, won: after have, say won.
Who won the game yesterday?
I never win at cards.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to play a short word game with you. After it, say who won: I won, or you won.

words.meaning: Get bigger, like a plant or a child.
words.example: The tree has grown very tall.
practice: Have you ever grown a plant?
Vegetables grow in the garden.
Grow, grown: the tree has grown.
Trees grow slowly, but they grow very tall.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor one thing you have grown, or one thing you have never grown. Ask it to check grown after have.

words.meaning: What you will do later: the day, the time and the place.
words.example: What is your plan for Saturday?
practice: Our plan is a walk to the lake.
Here is the plan: lunch at one, then the beach.
Will you tell me your plan?
We plan a day at the beach.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor: What is your plan for Saturday? Then tell it a plan of your own, real or made up, with will.

words.meaning: You and one or more people, in the same place.
words.example: Shall we walk together?
practice: We have lunch together on Sunday.
Shall we go to the park together?
My friend and I study together.
They work together in the office.
words.tutor: Give the tutor three ideas with Shall we … together? Ask it to answer each one.

words.meaning: Not yes and not no. It can happen, or not.
words.example: Maybe I will go to the beach.
practice: Shall we swim? Maybe later.
Maybe it will rain tomorrow.
Will you come? Maybe.
Maybe we can go together.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor three Will you…? questions. Answer one with yes, one with no, and one with maybe.

words.meaning: It says what you must do or must not do.
words.example: The rule is: no phones in the library.
practice: Rule 1: you must wear a helmet.
What are the rules at the pool?
You must not break the rules.
Read the rules on the sign.
words.tutor: Name a place for the tutor: a pool, a park or a library. Ask it for two rules there, then say one more yourself.

words.meaning: A hard hat. You wear it on a bike. It makes you safe.
words.example: My helmet is red and black.
practice: On a bike, you must wear a helmet.
Where is my helmet? It is next to the door.
Put on your helmet before the ride.
One helmet, two helmets.
words.tutor: Describe a helmet to the tutor, real or made up, with two colour words. Then say one rule with helmet and must.

words.meaning: Things to wear. All the people at a school or a job wear the same.
words.example: At some schools, you must wear a uniform.
practice: The nurse has a blue uniform.
Police officers wear a uniform.
Her uniform is clean and new.
What colour is the uniform at the park?
words.tutor: Tell the tutor about a uniform, real or made up. Say the job and the colours.

grammar.title: Have you ever…? I have, I have never
grammar.explanation:
Talk about things you have done, at any time before now.
Have you ever…? asks about any time, before now.
Answer: Yes, I have. Or: No, I haven't.
With he and she, use has: She has tried it.
grammar.rule:
Have you ever climbed a mountain?
Yes, I have.
No, I haven't.

I have climbed a mountain.
I have never climbed a mountain.
She has tasted this fruit.
He has never been to an island.

The word after have:
climb: climbed
try: tried
taste: tasted
see: seen
eat: eaten
grow: grown
fly: flown
win: won
go to a place: been

A time word, like last year? Use the past:
I climbed it last year.
grammar.workedExample:
Have you ever ___ fish for breakfast? (eat)
1. The question has have in it.
2. So the next word needs its have form.
3. Eat changes: eat, ate, eaten.
4. After have, use eaten. Not ate.
5. Have you ever eaten fish for breakfast?
6. Answer: Yes, I have. Or: No, I haven't.
7. Check: a question mark at the end. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use the past after have.
No: I have ate fish for breakfast.
Yes: I have eaten fish for breakfast.
No: Have you ever saw the sea?
Yes: Have you ever seen the sea?
grammar.tip: Have, then the have form: seen, eaten, been.
grammar.practice:
Write the right form of the word.
1. I have ___ a new fruit. (taste)
2. Have you ever ___ a tree? (climb)
3. She has ___ the sea. (see)
4. I have never ___ a game of cards. (win)
5. He has ___ vegetables in his garden. (grow)
6. Have you ever ___ to a desert? (go)
7. We have ___ fish for breakfast. (eat)
8. Have you ever ___ a new kind of bread? (try)
grammar.answers:
1. tasted  2. climbed  3. seen  4. won  5. grown  6. been  7. eaten  8. tried
Wrong on 6? For a place, use been: Have you ever been to a desert?
Wrong on 3 or 7? See and eat change: seen, eaten. Not saw or ate.
Wrong on 8? Try: the y changes to i, then -ed.

grammar.title: Shall we…? Will you…? Ideas and plans
grammar.explanation:
Shall we…? gives an idea for you and other people.
Will you…? asks a person about their plan.
Answer Will you…? with Yes, I will or No, I won't.
grammar.rule:
Give an idea:
Shall we go to the lake?
Shall we walk together?
Shall we have lunch now?

Answer an idea:
Yes, good idea!
OK, sure.
Maybe later.
Sorry, I can't.

Ask about a plan:
Will you come on Saturday?
Yes, I will.
No, I won't.
Won't: will not.

What will you do at the weekend?
I will visit my aunt. Maybe I will cook.
grammar.workedExample:
You want a walk near the river with a friend.
1. It is an idea for you and a friend: Shall we.
2. After shall we, the word stays the same: walk.
3. Shall we walk near the river?
4. Now ask about your friend's plan: Will you.
5. Will you come on Sunday?
6. Check: no to and no -ing after shall or will.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use shall with you.
No: Shall you come on Sunday?
Yes: Will you come on Sunday?
Use shall with we: Shall we go?
grammar.tip: An idea for us: Shall we? A plan for you: Will you?
grammar.practice:
Write Shall we or Will you.
1. ___ go to the beach on Saturday?
2. ___ come to the park with us? Yes, I will.
3. It is hot. ___ swim in the lake?
4. ___ be at home tomorrow? No, I won't.
5. ___ eat together tonight?
6. ___ visit your uncle on Friday? Yes, I will.
7. Now finish the answer: Will you come? No, I ___.
grammar.answers:
1. Shall we  2. Will you  3. Shall we  4. Will you  5. Shall we  6. Will you  7. won't
How to tell: an idea for you and others is Shall we. A question about one person's plan is Will you.
Wrong on 2, 4 or 6? The answer says I will or I won't, so the question is Will you.

grammar.title: Must and must not: rules and signs
grammar.explanation:
Must says: you need to do this. It is a rule.
Must not says: do not do this.
After must, the word stays the same, like after can.
grammar.rule:
At the pool:
You must have a shower first.
You must not run.

On a bike:
You must wear a helmet.

At the library:
You must not eat or drink.

At some schools and jobs:
You must wear a uniform.

He must, she must, they must.
Must has no s, and no to after it.
grammar.workedExample:
A sign at a lake says: No swimming.
1. No swimming: do not swim here.
2. It is a rule that says no: must not.
3. After must not, the word stays the same: swim.
4. You must not swim in the lake.
5. Check: no -ing and no to after must. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to put to after must.
No: You must to wear a helmet.
Yes: You must wear a helmet.
Must works like can: no to, and no s.
grammar.tip: Must, then the word as it is: must wear, must not run.
grammar.practice:
Write must or must not.
1. On a bike, you ___ wear a helmet.
2. In the library, you ___ talk loudly.
3. At the pool, you ___ run.
4. At some jobs, you ___ wear a uniform.
5. In the park, you ___ walk on the plants.
6. On a bus, you ___ pay for a ticket.
grammar.answers:
1. must  2. must not  3. must not  4. must  5. must not  6. must
A rule that says do this: must. A rule that says do not do this: must not.
Wrong on 2? Talking is OK. Talking loudly is not: you must not talk loudly.

grammar.title: Could, couldn't: can in the past
grammar.explanation:
Could is can, in the past.
Now: I can swim.
When I was six: I couldn't swim.
The l in could is quiet. Could sounds like good.
grammar.rule:
Now: I can ride a bike.
The past: When I was eight, I could ride a bike.

I couldn't read at three.
She could swim at five.
We couldn't see the lake last night.

Couldn't: could not.

Could you swim at ten?
Yes, I could.
No, I couldn't.

After could, the word stays the same:
could swim, could climb, could see.
grammar.workedExample:
Tomas at ten: ride a bike, yes. Swim, no.
1. At ten is in the past: could, not can.
2. Ride a bike, yes: could.
3. When Tomas was ten, he could ride a bike.
4. Swim, no: couldn't.
5. He couldn't swim.
6. Check: ride and swim stay the same after could. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to keep can for the past.
No: When I was ten, I can swim.
Yes: When I was ten, I could swim.
The word after could stays the same: could see, not could saw.
grammar.practice:
Write can, can't, could or couldn't.
1. When I was five, I ___ read. I learned at six.
2. Now I ___ read English.
3. Last year Dan ___ swim. Now he can.
4. When she was ten, she ___ ride a bike. She went to school on it.
5. It was night. We ___ see the river.
6. ___ you climb trees when you were eight? Yes, I could.
grammar.answers:
1. couldn't  2. can  3. couldn't  4. could  5. couldn't  6. Could
Wrong on 2? Now is not the past, so use can.
Wrong on 3? Now he can, so last year he couldn't.

grammar.title: What kind of…? How long…? How far…?
grammar.explanation:
Three new questions.
What kind of…? asks which group. Here, kind is not kind and friendly.
How long…? asks how much time, or how many metres from end to end.
How far…? asks: is it near or far from here?
grammar.rule:
What kind of music do you like?
I like film music.
What kind of tree is that?
It is an apple tree.

How long is the film?
Two hours.
How long is the bridge?
It is 300 metres long.

How far is the beach?
It is 500 metres from here.
Is it far? No, it is near.

With do: What kind of films do you like?
With is: How far is the lake?
grammar.workedExample:
You want to walk to the lake. Is it near or far?
1. Near or far: How far.
2. The lake is one thing: is.
3. How far is the lake?
4. Answer: It is 800 metres from here.
5. Check: a question mark at the end. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to leave out do.
No: What kind of music you like?
Yes: What kind of music do you like?
For he or she, use does: What kind of food does she like?
grammar.tip: Kind: which group. Long: time or metres. Far: from here.
grammar.practice:
Write What kind of, How long or How far.
1. ___ is the station? It is 2,000 metres from here.
2. ___ animals live in the desert? Birds and small animals.
3. ___ is the film? Two hours.
4. ___ bread do you want? Brown bread, please.
5. ___ is the walk to the lake? One hour.
6. ___ is the beach? It is near: 600 metres.
7. Make the question: you / what kind of / like / music / do
grammar.answers:
1. How far  2. What kind of  3. How long  4. What kind of  5. How long  6. How far  7. What kind of music do you like?
How long or how far? Metres from here to there: How far. Time, or metres from end to end: How long.
Wrong on 7? Do comes before you: do you like.

readings.title: Have You Ever Been to the Lake?
readings.setting: Two friends make a plan for Saturday on their phones.
readings.passage:
Eva: Hi Dan! Have you ever been to the lake near the forest?
Dan: No, I haven't. I have seen it in photos. It looks beautiful.
Eva: Shall we go on Saturday? We can ride our bikes.
Dan: Good idea! How long is the ride?
Eva: It takes one hour on a bike.
Dan: OK. Do I need a helmet?
Eva: Yes. You must wear a helmet on the road.
Dan: When I was ten, I could ride for hours. Now I get tired quickly!
Eva: We can stop at the lake and have lunch together.
Dan: Will you bring the food?
Eva: Yes, I will. I will bring bread, fruit and water.
Dan: Maybe we can swim in the lake too!
Eva: Maybe. The water is very cold in May.

readings.title: Kinds of Places in Nature
readings.setting: A page about places in nature.
readings.passage:
There are many kinds of places in nature.
A forest has a lot of trees. Many animals and birds live there.
A mountain is very tall. It is cold at the top, and there can be snow.
A river is a long line of water. It goes to the sea or to a lake.
The sea has salt in its water. Many lakes do not.
An island has water on every side.
A beach is next to the sea or a lake. People sit, walk and swim there.
A desert does not get much rain. Some plants can grow there. They do not need much water.

readings.title: A Sign at Lake Park
readings.setting: A sign at the gate of a big park with a lake.
readings.passage:
LAKE PARK
Open every day, 7 in the morning to 8 in the evening.

WALKS
Forest walk: 45 minutes
Lake walk: 1 hour 30 minutes
Beach: 900 metres from this sign

RULES
On a bike, you must wear a helmet.
You must not swim in the lake. You can swim at the beach.
You must not walk on the plants.
Put paper and bottles in the bins.

Questions? Ask a park worker. Park workers wear a green uniform.

comprehension.q: Has Dan ever been to the lake?
comprehension.a: No, he hasn't. He has seen it in photos.
comprehension.why: Dan says: No, I haven't. I have seen it in photos.

comprehension.q: How long is the ride to the lake?
comprehension.why: Eva says: It takes one hour on a bike.

comprehension.q: Dan says: When I was ten, I could ride for hours. Is this about now or the past?
comprehension.a: The past. Could is can in the past.
comprehension.why: When I was ten is the past. Now, Dan says, he gets tired quickly.
Dan asks: Will you bring the food? Eva says: Yes, I will.

comprehension.q: Which place has water on every side?
comprehension.why: Line 6: An island has water on every side.

comprehension.a: To the sea or to a lake.
comprehension.why: Line 4: It goes to the sea or to a lake.

comprehension.q: Some plants can grow in a desert. Why?
comprehension.a: They do not need much water.
comprehension.why: The last line: A desert does not get much rain. The plants there do not need much water.

comprehension.q: You are on a bike in Lake Park. What must you wear?
comprehension.why: The sign says: On a bike, you must wear a helmet.

comprehension.q: You want to swim. Where can you go, and how far is it?
comprehension.a: To the beach. It is 900 metres from the sign.
comprehension.why: You must not swim in the lake. You can swim at the beach. Beach: 900 metres from this sign.

comprehension.q: You have a question in the park. Who can you ask?
comprehension.a: A park worker in a green uniform.
comprehension.why: The sign says: Ask a park worker. Park workers wear a green uniform.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Have you ever…?
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
Have you ever climbed a mountain?
Yes, I have.
Have you ever tasted a new fruit?
No, I haven't.
I have seen the sea.
I have never been to a desert.
Tap the mic. Say the 6 lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: have at the start of each question? Seen and been, not saw and went?
speaking.tutor: Say the six lines to the tutor. Then ask it three new Have you ever…? questions, and answer the three it asks you.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Things I have done
speaking.instructions:
Say 5 lines about you.
I have ___.
I have ___.
I have ___ and ___.
I have never ___.
I have never ___.
Pick from: climbed a tree, tasted a new fruit, grown a plant.
Or: won a game, been to an island, seen a river.
Each line can be true or made up.
Tap the mic. Say it. Tap again. Listen.
Check: 5 lines? Never in 2 of them? The have form after have?
speaking.instructionsSpeech:
Say 5 lines about you.
I have …
I have …
I have … and …
I have never …
I have never …
Pick from: climbed a tree, tasted a new fruit, grown a plant.
Or: won a game, been to an island, seen a river.
Each line can be true or made up.
Tap the mic. Say it. Tap again. Listen.
Check: 5 lines? Never in 2 of them? The have form after have?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your five lines. Ask it to ask you Have you ever…? about two of them, and answer with Yes, I have or No, I haven't.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — What kind? How long? How far?
speaking.instructions:
Listen to each question. Say your answer.
What kind of music do you like?
What kind of food do you like?
How long is your favourite film?
How long is a football game?
How far is the nearest shop?
Answer with a full line: I like …, or It is … .
Your answers can be true or made up.
Tap the mic. Say the 5 answers. Tap again. Listen.
Check: kind, a group. Long, time or metres. Far, metres from here.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to ask you six questions with What kind of, How long and How far, in any order. Answer each with a full line.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Could, couldn't, must
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat.
Could: the l is quiet. Could sounds like good.
I could swim when I was six.
Couldn't: could and not, in one word.
I couldn't read at three.
Must: the u sounds like the u in bus.
You must wear a helmet.
Tap the mic. Say the 6 lines. Tap again. Listen.
Check: no l sound in could? Must like bus?
speaking.tutor: Say could and good, then must and bus, to the tutor. Ask it: does each pair have the same middle sound?

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Shall we go together?
speaking.instructions:
Read A. Say B.
1. A: Shall we go to the beach on Saturday? B: Yes, good idea! Will you bring the water?
2. A: Shall we walk to the river? B: Maybe later. I am tired now.
3. A: Will you come to the park with us? B: Sorry, I can't. I am busy.
4. A: Shall we have lunch together? B: OK, sure. Shall we meet at one o'clock?
5. A: What will you do at the weekend? B: I will visit my family. Maybe I will cook.
Tap the mic. Say the 5 B lines. Tap again. Listen.
Now start one: say a new A line with Shall we, then answer it.
Check: shall with we? After Will you, I will or I won't?
A friend can say A. No one with you? Say A and B.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor an idea with Shall we…? and let it answer. Then let it ask you Will you…? and answer. Do three turns each.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — At the park desk
speaking.instructions:
You are at the desk of a big park. You ask the questions.
You: Hello. How far is the lake from here?
Desk: It is 900 metres. Turn left at the café.
You: How long is the forest walk?
Desk: It is 45 minutes.
You: What kind of animals live in the forest?
Desk: Birds, and some small animals.
You: Can I ride my bike there?
Desk: Yes, but you must wear a helmet.
You: Thanks. Goodbye!
Tap the mic. Say your lines. Tap again. Listen.
Now ask about the beach. Change one question.
Check: How far, How long and What kind of in your lines?
A friend can read the desk lines. No one with you? Read them, then say yours.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the person at the park desk. Ask it How far, How long and What kind of questions, and listen for must in its answers.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Have you ever…?
writing.prompt:
Write 4 sentences about things you have done.
Write 2 with I have and 2 with I have never.
They can be true or made up.
writing.model:
I have climbed a tall tree.
I have eaten fish for breakfast.
I have never been to a desert.
I have never grown a plant.
writing.criteria:
4 sentences.
2 with I have. 2 with I have never.
The have form after have: seen, eaten, been. Not saw, ate, went.
A capital letter and a full stop in each.
writing.support:
Copy the model.
Change the last two words only.
Check each have form with the list on Pattern 1.
writing.extension: Write one question for a friend: Have you ever…? Then write your own answer: Yes, I have or No, I haven't.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Then and now
writing.prompt:
Write 4 sentences.
2 about what you could or couldn't do when you were younger.
2 about what you can or can't do now.
They can be true or made up.
writing.model:
When I was six, I couldn't swim.
Now I can swim.
When I was five, I couldn't read.
Now I can read English.
writing.criteria:
4 sentences: 2 with could or couldn't, 2 with can or can't.
When I was in each could sentence.
The word after could stays the same: could swim, not could swam.
writing.support:
Start with one pair.
When I was six, I couldn't ___. Now I can ___.
Put the same word in both gaps.
writing.extension: Add a line about a friend: When he was ten, he could … .

writing.title: Writing 3 — Rules for a place
writing.prompt:
Write 4 rules for one place: a pool, a library, a park or a bike ride.
Write 2 with must and 2 with must not.
writing.model:
THE LIBRARY: RULES
You must bring your library card.
You must put the books on the shelf.
You must not eat or drink.
You must not talk loudly.
writing.criteria:
A title with the name of the place.
4 rules: 2 with must, 2 with must not.
No to after must.
Each rule starts with You and ends with a full stop.
writing.support:
Look at the sign in Reading 3.
Copy one rule.
Now change the place and one word in it.
writing.extension: Add one line: Questions? Ask a worker in a … uniform.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A message with a plan
writing.prompt:
Write a message to a friend or someone in your family.
Give an idea for a day out with Shall we…?
Ask a question with How far or How long.
Ask about their plan with Will you…?
Add one line with must.
You can use a made-up name.
writing.model:
Hi Priya,
Shall we go to the forest on Sunday?
How long is the walk to the lake?
Will you bring some water?
We must take a map.
See you soon! Tomas
writing.length: A hello, four lines and a name
writing.criteria:
A hello line and a name at the end.
One Shall we question and one Will you question.
One How far or How long question.
One line with must.
A question mark after each question.
writing.support:
Copy the model.
Change the place and the day.
Then change one more word in each line.
writing.extension: Add a line with maybe: Maybe we can swim in the lake.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Have or has, and the right form
activities.instructions:
Write have or has, and the right form of the word.
1. I ___ ___ the sea. (see)
2. She ___ ___ a mountain. (climb)
3. We ___ never ___ to a desert. (go)
4. He ___ ___ vegetables in his garden. (grow)
5. They ___ ___ a new kind of fruit. (taste)
6. ___ you ever ___ fish for breakfast? (eat)
7. ___ she ever ___ a football game? (win)
8. I ___ never ___ this food. (try)
activities.answers:
1. have seen  2. has climbed  3. have, been  4. has grown  5. have tasted  6. Have, eaten  7. Has, won  8. have, tried
Has for he, she and it. Have for I, you, we and they.
Wrong on 3? For a place, go takes been: We have never been to a desert.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 1 and do it again.
activities.solo: Write your answers on paper. Check each one with the key. Count the right ones.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Match the word
activities.instructions:
Match 1 to 10 with a to j.
1. island
2. desert
3. lake
4. river
5. forest
6. beach
7. mountain
8. helmet
9. uniform
10. plant
a. It is long. It goes to the sea.
b. A lot of trees in one place.
c. It has water on every side.
d. It does not get much rain.
e. Very big and tall. It can have snow on top.
f. Big water in one place, but not the sea.
g. Next to the sea. You can sit and swim there.
h. A hard hat for a bike.
i. The same things to wear for all the people at a job.
j. A green thing that grows. It needs water and sun.
activities.answers:
1c  2d  3f  4a  5b  6g  7e  8h  9i  10j
Check 1 and 3: an island is in the water. A lake is the water.
9 or 10 right: good.
8 or less: go back to Words, listen again, and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each word out loud. Write the letter. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Shall we or Will you?
activities.instructions:
Part A. Write Shall we or Will you.
1. ___ walk to the beach together?
2. ___ be at home at six?
3. ___ try the new café?
4. ___ come to the party on Friday?
Part B. Write the right answer.
5. Shall we climb the mountain? (Good idea! / Yes, I will.)
6. Will you visit your aunt? (No, I won't. / Good idea!)
7. Shall we eat now? (Maybe later. / No, I won't.)
8. Will you come with us? (Yes, I will. / Yes, we shall.)
activities.answers:
1. Shall we  2. Will you  3. Shall we  4. Will you  5. Good idea!  6. No, I won't.  7. Maybe later.  8. Yes, I will.
An idea gets Good idea, OK or Maybe later. A Will you question gets I will or I won't.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 2 and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each line out loud with your answer. Write it. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Read the sign, write the rule
activities.instructions:
Read each sign. Write must or must not.
1. POOL: No running. You ___ run.
2. BIKES: Helmets, please. You ___ wear a helmet.
3. LIBRARY: Quiet, please. You ___ talk loudly.
4. SHOP WORKERS: Green uniform, please. Workers ___ wear a green uniform.
5. PARK: Please do not walk on the plants. You ___ walk on the plants.
6. LAKE: No swimming. You ___ swim here.
7. BUS: Tickets, please. You ___ have a ticket.
8. Now write your own rule for one place, with must or must not.
activities.answers:
1. must not  2. must  3. must not  4. must  5. must not  6. must not  7. must
8. Your own rule. Example: At the cinema, you must not talk. Check: must, then the word as it is.
No or do not on the sign: must not. Please, or a thing you need: must.
6 or 7 right of 1 to 7: good.
5 or less: read Pattern 3 and do it again.
activities.solo: Read each sign out loud. Write your rule. Check with the key. For 8, check the word after must has no to and no -ing.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Can or could?
activities.instructions:
Write can, can't, could or couldn't.
1. When I was three, I ___ read. Now I can.
2. Now I ___ swim. I learned last year.
3. Last night it was cold. We ___ sleep.
4. When he was nine, he ___ climb tall trees.
5. ___ you ride a bike when you were six? Yes, I could.
6. Mia ___ come yesterday. She was busy.
7. Today I am free. I ___ come with you.
8. When she was young, she ___ grow vegetables in her garden.
activities.answers:
1. couldn't  2. can  3. couldn't  4. could  5. Could  6. couldn't  7. can  8. could
When I was, last night and yesterday are the past: could or couldn't. Now and today: can or can't.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 4 and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each line out loud with your word. Write the word. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Make the question
activities.instructions:
Make a question.
Start with a capital letter.
End with a question mark.
1. kind / what / of / music / you / do / like
2. far / how / is / the / beach
3. long / how / is / the / film
4. ever / have / you / climbed / a mountain
5. we / shall / go / together
6. will / come / you / on Friday
7. of / kind / what / tree / is / that
activities.answers:
1. What kind of music do you like?
2. How far is the beach?
3. How long is the film?
4. Have you ever climbed a mountain?
5. Shall we go together?
6. Will you come on Friday?
7. What kind of tree is that?
Number 1: do comes before you.
Number 4: ever goes after you and before climbed.
6 or 7 right: good.
5 or less: read Patterns 1, 2 and 5 and do it again.
activities.solo: Write each question. Read it out loud. Check with the key.

quizzes.why: After have, use the have form: seen. Saw is the past, for a time like yesterday. See and seeing are not the have form.

quizzes.q: Have you ever climbed a mountain? Which short answer is right?
quizzes.why: A question with have gets have in the answer. No goes with haven't. Didn't and don't answer other questions. No, I have says no and yes.
She takes has: she has tasted. Have is for I, you, we and they. Is and did do not go before tasted here.

options: I have went to a desert.
I have go to a desert.
I have been to a desert.
quizzes.a: I have been to a desert.
quizzes.why: For a place, the have form of go is been. Went is the past, not the have form. Go has no new form. I been has no have.

quizzes.q: You want a walk with a friend. Which line gives the idea?
options: Shall we walk to the river?
Shall you walk to the river?
Shall we walking to the river?
We walk shall to the river?
quizzes.a: Shall we walk to the river?
quizzes.why: Shall we gives an idea. Shall goes with we, not you. After shall we, no -ing. Shall comes first in the question.

quizzes.q: Will you come on Saturday? You can't come. What do you say?
quizzes.why: Will you gets will or won't. You can't come, so: No, I won't. Yes, I will says you can come. Good idea answers Shall we. Don't answers a do question.

quizzes.q: On a bike, you ___ wear a helmet.
quizzes.why: It is a rule to wear a helmet, so: must. No to after must. Must has no s. Must not says do not wear it, and that is not the rule.

quizzes.q: A sign at the lake says: No swimming. What does it mean?
quizzes.why: No swimming is a rule that says do not swim: must not. Must swim says the opposite. Could is the past of can. Shall we gives an idea, not a rule.

quizzes.q: When I was six, I ___ swim. I learned at eight.
quizzes.why: At six is the past, and you learned later, so: couldn't. Can't is for now. Could says yes, but you could not swim then. Don't is not the past.

quizzes.q: In which word is the l quiet?
quizzes.why: Could has a quiet l. It sounds like good. You say the l in lake, plan and helmet.

quizzes.q: ___ is the beach? It is 500 metres from here.
quizzes.why: Metres from here to there: How far. How long asks about time, or a thing from end to end. What kind of asks which group. How old asks about years.

quizzes.q: What kind of place is a desert?
options: A place with a lot of trees.
A place with water on every side.
A place next to the sea.
A place with not much rain.
quizzes.a: A place with not much rain.
quizzes.why: A desert does not get much rain. A lot of trees is a forest. Water on every side is an island. Next to the sea is a beach.

teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. If you are helping, listen to the recordings together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence.

teacherNotes.type: The one error worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: The past form creeps in after have and after could: I have saw, I have went, I could swam. The learner already knows saw, went and ate from Units 10 and 16, so the more confident they are with the past, the more often this appears. When you hear it, point at the word before it, have or could, and let them fix the verb. Been is taught as the have form of go for places; gone is deliberately left out.

No task asks whether the learner has really done anything. Every Have you ever… task allows a true or an invented answer, and no task touches travel, countries, flying in a plane or money. Nature places are kinds of place and are never named. Please keep it that way if you add your own questions, and never correct a made-up answer.

Present perfect here is only for experiences, with ever and never; yet, just and since are not taught here. Could is taught only as the past of can; Could you help me? as a polite request, and Shall I…? as an offer, are real English but not taught here. Must is not compared with have to. Because, to for a purpose and by bus come in Unit 19, so the unit avoids them.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task is scored by it alone. The learner is told throughout that made-up names and made-up answers are fine. Keep that wording, and never ask the learner to give the tutor real personal details, such as where they live or where they have travelled.

selfAssessment.statement: I can ask Have you ever…? and answer it.
I can write: I have tasted it. I have never been there.
I can give an idea with Shall we…? and answer Will you…?
I can read a sign and say what I must and must not do.
I can say what I could and couldn't do in the past.
I can answer What kind of…? How long…? How far…?
I can write a message with a plan and a rule.

assignment.title: Have you ever? Shall we?
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Tap the mic. Say two things you have done and one thing you have never done. Say one thing you could do when you were younger. Give an idea with Shall we…? Say one rule with must.
2. Write a message like Writing 4: an idea, a How far or How long question, a Will you question and a rule.
You can use a made-up name. Your answers can be made up.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written message
